DEMOCRACY - How does USAID promote democracy abroad when we are faced with so
many challenges here at home? How will you rebuild US credibility for democracy promotion
abroad? Given that the Trump Administration cut democracy funds, what will you do to
adequately resource this important work?
• As President Biden has noted in his inaugural address, "We will lead not merely by the
example of our power, but the power of our example." I firmly believe that USAID's
democracy assistance can embrace--and be strenothened by--the example of our own
democracy's resilience. If confirmed, I will conver that the most powerful and
enduring contribution to "democracy promotion" is the model we provide to others on
our own commitment to these core principles.
• Healthy democracy is not a system without challenges, but a svstem designed to
effectivelv manage the challenges it inevitably has. And as all of us in this hearing
know, our nation's democracy has faced challenges at everv turn in its historv, many
more dire than the ones we confront now. Fortunatelv, guided bv our Constitution's
enduring pursuit of a "more perfect Union," our democracy has weathered and
overcome challenges for more than 200 vears, often after long, hiahly contested and
bitterly fought strugales.
• By desion, our democracy has become more responsive and inclusive over time and
dealt with challenges that could not have been envisioned by the original framers. And
in a sense. that's the basic distillation and inspiration for a core premise of DRG
technical assistance: our purpose is not to replicate the form of American institutions
abroad, but to instill the commitment and ability of partner institutions to learn.
respond and adapt to changing needs and circumstances.
• If confirmed. I will encourage providing assistance with more humility and empathy in our
work. While autocrats in Moscow. Beijing, Tehran and elsewhere seize on our own
domestic challenges as evidence of American weakness and hvpocrisv, those in the
democracy promotion space believe that acknowledoing our own challenges and
examining those issues, is an axiomatic aspect of American democracy and precisely
what distinguishes us from autocracies.
• If confirmed, I will continue to champion USAID in applying three principal approaches to
supporting civil society in restrictive environments: prevention, adaptation and innovation.
• Many restrictive governments are using COVID-19 as an excuse to incorporate further
restrictions. USAID recognizes that these restrictions have increased threats to civil society.
As COVID-19 began to spread globally. USAID partners were among the first to
highlight that it was not just a public health crisis. but also a crisis for civic space. In
just over two weeks after the WHO officially declared a pandemic. ICNL and the
European Center for Nonprofit Law (ECNL) launched the COVID-19 Civic Freedom
Tracker. assessing 164 countries and more than 400 measures - emergency
declarations, laws, and practices that affect the freedoms of association, assembly. and
expression.

DEMOCRACY - How does USAID stem corruption in the countries in which it works?
• As the outset, I'd like to stress the importance of USAID's work in helping countries
prevent and fight corruption, as well as enhance transparency, accountability and good
governance. Corruption and related crime and kleptocracy are on the rise around the world.
undermining development outcomes across all sectors and perpetuating a cycle of poverty
and dependency. At USAID, we know that corruption diverts resources from essential
public services; undermines democratic norms and institutions; diminishes citizen trust;
drives human rights violations; and allows corrupt actors to profit from crime, terror and
exploitation. It impacts USAID's ability to meet our objectives in health, education,
economic growth, climate change, and biodiversity. And sadly, as shown by COVID-19
related corruption, it also impacts the response to global health and other emergencies.
• USAID's approach to combating corruption reflects our understanding of it as both a system
and a norm. Our programs aim to replace the practices, drivers, incentives and behaviors that
feed systemic corruption with ones that instead build systemic accountability to citizens.
• USAID programs in countries such as El Salvador, Ukraine, the Philippines, Haiti, and
Ghana are supporting systems and practices that build the capacity of governing institutions
to prevent, detect, investigate, and sanction corruption. This includes enhancing oversight of
public spending, strengthening asset declaration, supporting anti-corruption agencies, and
building the capacity of government auditors. Other programs strengthen justice sector
institutions and anti-corruption courts, enhance inter-govermental coordination, and build
the capacity of prosecutors, judges, law enforcement and investigators to detect and combat
financial crime and corruption.
• On the governance side, our programs in countries such as Jordan, Albania, Sri Lanka and
Uganda support public administration tools aimed at preventing corruption, including e-

Georgia and Paraguay we are leveraging technology, access to information laws, and open

• Anti-corruption programming remains a key technical priority of USAID's democracy and
governance work around the world. Yet despite the critical nature of this work to securing
both democracy and broader development outcomes, USAID funding levels for anti-
corruption have declined consistently in the past few years, with 2020 funding levels a full
44% lower than in 2017. If confirmed, I will prioritize replenished funding in this area, so
that anti-corruption work at USAID can be re-invigorated and re-elevated.
DEMOCRACY - Do you believe there is duplication of democracy assistance implemented by
USAID, the National Endowment for Democracy, and the Department of State's Bureau of
Democracy, Human Rights and Labor, International Narcotics Law Enforcement and
Conflict and Stabilization Operations Bureaus, and if so, what will you do about it?
• USAID manages most of the US government's democracy assistance funding and supports
the broadest range of democracy, human rights and governance programming, but the
National Endowment for Democracy and the Department of State also play important roles
in the United States' overall efforts to promote and defend democracy around the world.
• While there is some overlap, each entity has distinct comparative advantages, giving the US
a multi-faceted and more effective approach in increasingly complex environments.
• Furthermore, I understand that there is regular information-sharing and coordination efforts
to avoid duplication and help make the most strategic use of assistance funds. This
coordination takes place both in DC and at our missions overseas.
• That being said, more can be done to strengthen orchestration of effort among US
